items.title: VPN on iPhone: What the Setting Means and How to Set One Up
items.summary: The VPN line in your iPhone’s Settings shows whether a VPN is carrying your internet traffic. “Connected” means it is. That line only appears once something has added a VPN configuration to the phone: a VPN app, your employer or school, or a security app that borrows the same slot. iOS doesn’t come with a VPN service. It comes with the switch. If the switch turned itself on and you never set up a VPN, chapter 2 has the short answer. New to VPNs? Start with what a VPN is . Are VPNs Safe? What Has Gone Wrong, What Has Held Up
items.summary: A VPN from a company with a checkable record is safe to use, and legal in most countries. The risk is the company itself, because it sees the traffic you’re hiding from everyone else. That’s the trade at the heart of every VPN. Your internet provider, the café Wi-Fi and the sites you visit see less, and one company sees more. Most of the time that company keeps its word. Sometimes it hasn’t, and both kinds of story are on the public record: court files, police searches, leaked databases, audit reports. items.title: Do You Need a VPN? An Honest Answer for Each Situation
items.summary: Not for everyday browsing at home. You need one when the network you’re on shouldn’t see where you go, or blocks where you want to go. That covers fewer situations than VPN ads suggest, and a few more than the skeptics admit. Almost every site now encrypts what you send, so the old picture of a stranger reading your bank password over café Wi-Fi is mostly out of date. What’s left is quieter: the café, the hotel, your internet provider or a government can still see which sites you visit, and some of them block the ones you need. items.title: What Is a VPN? How It Works and What It Won’t Hide
items.summary: A VPN (virtual private network) is a service that sends your internet traffic through an encrypted tunnel to a server run by the VPN company. Websites then see that server’s IP address, not yours. That one change cuts both ways. Your internet provider, and whoever runs the Wi-Fi you’re on, can no longer see which sites you visit. The VPN company now can, a detail most explanations leave out. The word also covers two different things. At work, a VPN connects your laptop into the company network so you can reach internal systems from home; that’s the original meaning, and the one in NIST’s defin…
